statement: In healthy volunteers given single analgesic amounts in crossover laboratory studies, how much of a ketamine dose reaches the bloodstream depends on the route. Measured against an intravenous dose in the same people, an intramuscular injection gave 93% (0.930, SE 0.026) and a swallowed solution 16.6% (0.166, SE 0.028), each the mean of four people, with a second calculation on all six people giving 19.5% (0.195, SE 0.028) for the swallowed solution (Clements et al., 1982). A later study of three men found 18.3% (SD 4.7) and 17.6% (SD 3.8), for the two mirror-image forms, after a swallowed tablet (Yanagihara et al., 2003), so a figure close to the 1982 one has been found by a second group, though not under the same condition: the earlier study used a solution drunk in orange juice and the later one two swallowed tablets, each measured against its own study's intravenous reference. The intramuscular figure has not been measured again in the sources read here, and the 2016 review repeats it beside a much larger intramuscular amount than the one at which it was measured. Blood levels rose fast after the intramuscular injection (peak 243 ng/mL, SE 49, at 22 minutes, SE 4; ketamine present in under 4 minutes; peaks between 100 and 425 ng/mL across people) and stayed low after the swallowed solution (peak 44 ng/mL, SE 10, range 15 to 80, at 30 minutes, SE 5). The 1982 abstract and results call the oral loss a failure to absorb, while the discussion of the same paper argues that absorption from the gut was complete and the drug was broken down in the liver before reaching the circulation; the metabolite figures in that paper support the discussion. Both headline figures rest on four people, the intravenous reference is described in a separate five-person study without saying who provided it, and no confidence interval appears anywhere in either paper. The time to peak the later study prints for the swallowed tablet cannot be reproduced from the sampling times that paper lists (study card sc_yanagihara_2003). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Almost all of a dose injected into a muscle reaches the blood: about 93 in every 100 parts, in one small study. When the same amount is swallowed, only about 17 in 100 gets there, because the liver breaks most of it down first. Both figures come from four people each. After a muscle injection the blood level peaks in about 20 minutes; after swallowing it peaks later and stays much lower. A later study of three men found about the same figure for swallowing.
population: Healthy fasting adult volunteers in two crossover laboratory studies reported together (5 people in the intravenous study, 6 in the intramuscular and oral study, with each bioavailability figure printed for 4 of them), and 3 healthy Japanese men aged 27 to 40 in the later study
exposure: A single amount of ketamine by one named route (study conditions: 0.25 and 0.125 mg of base per kg of body weight intravenously; 0.5 mg/kg as an intramuscular injection; 0.5 mg/kg as an oral solution in orange juice; and in the later study a 20 mg intravenous injection and a swallowed tablet containing 50 mg)
comparator: An intravenous dose in the same person as the reference for absolute availability, with saline on a separate occasion in the 1982 study
outcome: Share of the dose reaching the bloodstream (bioavailability), peak blood level and time to that peak
magnitude: Clements et al. (1982): intramuscular Farea 0.930 (SE 0.026, n=4 printed values 0.965, 0.923, 0.972, 0.859); oral Farea 0.166 (SE 0.028, n=4: 0.145, 0.163, 0.112, 0.245) and 0.195 (SE 0.028) from Eq. 2 across 6 people; intramuscular Cmax 243 ng/mL (SE 49) at tmax 22 min (SE 4); oral Cmax 44 ng/mL (SE 10) at 30 min (SE 5). Yanagihara et al. (2003), swallowed tablet in 3 men: bioavailability 18.3% (SD 4.7) for the (R)- and 17.6% (SD 3.8) for the (S)-enantiomer; Cmax 42.6 (SD 13.3) and 40.4 (SD 14.2) ng/mL at 33.3 (SD 15.3) and 30.0 (SD 30.0) min.

evidence.locator: Table I, columns Farea (intramuscular and oral) and F (Eq. 2)
evidence.extracted: Bioavailability against each person's own intravenous curve: intramuscular mean 0.930 (SE 0.026) from the four printed values 0.965, 0.923, 0.972 and 0.859; oral mean 0.166 (SE 0.028) from 0.145, 0.163, 0.112 and 0.245; the Eq. 2 estimate for the oral route is 0.195 (SE 0.028) from six values (0.160, 0.190, 0.155, 0.115, 0.309, 0.239). Two of the six people have no area-based value in either column and no reason is given.

Text figures: bioavailability after intramuscular injection 93%, with apparent absorption half-times of 2 to 17 minutes, a lag of under 4 minutes and apparent peak concentrations between 100 and 425 ng/mL at 5 to 30 minutes; after the oral solution only 16.6% of the dose reached the systemic circulation, with a lag of 4 to 13 minutes (mean 8.0) and a mean apparent peak of 44 ng/mL (range 15 to 80), against 243 ng/mL after the intramuscular injection.

By route (mean with SE): peak 243 ng/mL (49) at 22 min (4) after the intramuscular injection and 44 ng/mL (10) at 30 min (5) after the oral solution; dose-corrected area 27.5 (1.2) intravenous, 23.6 (2.2) intramuscular and 4.8 (0.8) oral; clearance 19.1 (1.1) and 23.2 (2.7) mL/min/kg. The table's footnote gives N = 6 for all three columns although the intravenous study is described in five people, and the printed unit for the areas is wrong by about a factor of a thousand, so the areas should not be quoted with it.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 539); Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs of the oral section (p. 541)
evidence.extracted: The abstract attributes the low oral figure to a failure to absorb, while the Discussion states that the similar norketamine areas after the oral and intravenous conditions show the loss happened in the liver on first pass, and the Eq. 2 estimate is made on the assumption that absorption from the gut lumen was complete. A claim about ketamine taken by mouth should follow the Discussion, not the abstract.
evidence.quote: only 17% of an oral dose was absorbed

evidence.locator: Table 1, tablet row (columns Cmax, Tmax and BA)
evidence.extracted: Swallowed tablet containing 50 mg in three men, against the same men's intravenous curves: bioavailability 18.3% (SD 4.7) for the (R)- and 17.6% (SD 3.8) for the (S)-enantiomer; peak 42.6 (SD 13.3) and 40.4 (SD 14.2) ng/mL at 33.3 (SD 15.3) and 30.0 (SD 30.0) minutes. Each figure is a mean of three men and no individual values are printed.

The review states, second-hand, that 17 to 24% of swallowed racemic ketamine and 8 to 11% of swallowed S-ketamine reach the circulation, citing six studies, and that peak concentrations come about 40 to 55 minutes after ingestion. The sample sizes behind these figures appear only in its Table 1 and never in the text.

The review carries the intramuscular figure of approximately 93% forward as a property of the drug and attaches it to an intramuscular amount several times larger than the one at which it was measured, which also contradicts its own table; it adds that the terminal half-life after an intramuscular injection does not differ significantly from the intravenous one and that ketamine is detectable in plasma after 4 minutes, with peaks within 5 to 30 minutes.

risk_of_bias.note: Order was randomized in the 1982 crossover and the two extravascular routes were masked against each other, but the method of randomization is not described, the assay is unvalidated in the report, both headline figures are printed for four of six people with no explanation, and the intravenous reference they are ratios to is described in a separate five-person study (card sc_clements_1982, overall high). The later tablet figure comes from an open, unrandomized study (card sc_yanagihara_2003, overall high).

inconsistency.note: The two independent oral estimates agree closely (16.6% and 19.5% against 18.3% and 17.6%), although they were made on different preparations; the intramuscular figure has no second measurement to disagree with.

indirectness.note: Bioavailability by route is measured directly in healthy volunteers, which is what the claim states.

imprecision.note: Four to six people in 1982 and three in 2003, with no confidence interval anywhere; the individual oral estimates run from 0.112 to 0.309 and intramuscular peak concentrations from 100 to 425 ng/mL.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from two small primary studies.

grade.reasoning: Within-person controlled-administration studies with an intravenous reference start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 for the missing individual data behind both headline figures, the untraceable intravenous reference and the unvalidated assay; imprecision −1 for four to six people per figure, three in the replication, and no intervals. Not downgraded for inconsistency, because the only route measured twice gave the same answer, or for indirectness. The status is replicated for the oral figure only, and for the number rather than the condition, because the two estimates come from different preparations (a solution and a tablet): the intramuscular figure of 93% rests on four people in one 1982 report and is still the figure reviews carry.

verification.flag_note: All anchors ai-located by the claim writer from the PDFs and not yet checked by a second reader. The Clements figures were read on the pages rendered at 150 dpi as well as in the text extraction, because that PDF is a scan.

changelog.change: New draft claim written from the first readers' cards and the PDFs of Clements et al. (1982) and Yanagihara et al. (2003), with the 2016 review as a second-hand qualifier. Split from the other routes (cl_ket_bioavailability_other_routes) because those rest on one three-person study and are rated lower.

Editor: status set to metadata-verified (every reference Crossref-verified and retraction-checked; not narrative-only). Every anchor is checked by a second reader (blind reconciliation and targeted checks): status ai-anchored (METHODS §12).

Review and adjudication, ketamine round: the absorption wording is the abstract's and the results' (second reader 224, checked at Clements 1982 pp. 539-540); 'found twice by different groups' qualified, because the 1982 oral condition was a solution and the 2003 one a swallowed tablet; the 2016 review's attachment of the 93% figure to a much larger intramuscular amount brought into the statement; the unreproducible printed time to peak for the swallowed tablet named.
Editor: closing sentence added to the statement giving its certainty and status, as every other answer's statement ends; no other change.
